R04-F-01: It is tempting to picture the great periodic fair of the pre-modern world as a market that happened to be very large. Merchants arrived with bales of cloth, casks and livestock; buyers came from the surrounding districts; for a few weeks a meadow outside a town became a crowded street of stalls, and then it emptied again until the following year. On this view the fair existed because trade was too thin to support permanent shops, and it faded once towns grew large enough to sustain them. The account is not wrong, but it describes the visible part of the fair and mistakes it for the whole. Much of what happened at a fair left no bales behind. Merchants who met there once or twice a year used the occasion to settle accounts that had been running since the previous meeting, cancelling what one owed another against what a third owed the first, so that relatively little coin had to change hands. Promises to pay at the next fair circulated as a kind of credit, and their value rested on the expectation that everyone would return. A fair, in this sense, was a calendar as much as a place: it fixed the dates on which obligations fell due and gave distant traders a reason to keep faith with one another. A merchant who failed to appear risked more than a season's sales; he risked his standing with every partner who had expected to meet him. It was also a clearing house for news. Prices in distant regions, the solvency of a trading house, a harvest failure, rumours of war: all of this travelled with the people who came, and a merchant who stayed at home was not only missing customers but trading blind. The gossip of the fair was not idle. It was the means by which a scattered commercial world kept a rough common picture of itself. A thinly attended fair was therefore a loss twice over, since the absence of buyers was also an absence of reports, and those who controlled the best information often profited more than those who carried the most goods. Seen this way, the decline of the great fairs looks different. Permanent shops certainly took over much of the retail business, but the deeper loss was of the fair's other functions, which passed to institutions that did not depend on bodily presence: banks that kept accounts all year round, regular postal services and, later, printed lists of prices. None of this means that fairs ceased to matter as markets; many survived for centuries as places to buy animals or household goods. What they lost was their role as the hinge on which a whole year of commerce turned, and that role had never been visible in the stalls.
R04-F-02: Few ideas feel more natural than the distinction between home and work. We leave one for the other in the morning and return in the evening, and much of our moral vocabulary depends on the contrast: home is where we are valued for who we are, work where we are valued for what we produce. Yet for most of recorded history, in most agrarian and artisan societies, the distinction would have puzzled the people who lived in households. The house was where the work was done. Consider a weaver's dwelling in a pre-industrial town, or a farmstead in the countryside. The looms or the dairy stood beside the hearth, and the people who ate at the table included not only parents and children but apprentices, servants and labourers who lived under the same roof and the same authority. The head of the household was at once father, employer and, in a limited sense, magistrate, answerable to the wider community for the conduct of everyone in his charge. Records of such households often used the word family to mean this whole working unit, and a reader who assumes that it meant blood relatives alone will misread them badly. Children worked as soon as they were able, carding wool or minding animals, and learning a trade was part of growing up in the house rather than something that began when a child left it. None of this should be romanticised. The working household was a hierarchy, often a harsh one, in which servants could be beaten and wives had little legal standing apart from their husbands. Nor was it universal: the poorest labourers, who owned no tools and rented a single room, had little to bring home but their wages. The point is not that the old arrangement was better, but that it was different in kind, and that the difference matters for how we read later history. When production moved into workshops, mills and offices, the household did not simply lose its economic role; it acquired a new meaning. Freed of the loom and the dairy, it could be imagined as a private refuge, governed by affection rather than discipline, and this ideal was then projected backwards as if it had always existed. The ideal was real enough for those who could afford it, but it was an ideal, not a description of the past. Laments about the decline of the family often rest on that projection. What changed over these centuries was less the strength of family feeling than the range of tasks the household was expected to perform, and a history that confuses the two will find decline where there was mainly transformation.
R04-F-03: Before the railways, every town kept its own time. Noon was the moment the sun stood highest over the local meridian, and because the sun appears to move westward, a town some distance to the west of another reached its noon a few minutes later. Nobody minded, because nothing travelled fast enough for the difference to matter; a coach journey of several days absorbed a quarter of an hour's discrepancy without anyone noticing it. The railway changed this, and the standard account of what followed is a story of practical necessity. Timetables drawn up in dozens of local times produced confusion and, on single-track lines, danger, so the companies adopted a single reference time and governments eventually followed. The account is true as far as it goes, but it treats the change as a technical adjustment, like agreeing on a common gauge for the rails. It was more than that. Local time had been public in a literal sense: anyone could see the sun, and the clock on the church or the town hall was set by an observation that a curious citizen could, in principle, check. Standard time was set somewhere else, by astronomers in a distant observatory, and reached the town along a telegraph wire. The hour on the station clock was no longer a fact about the place where one stood but a decision taken elsewhere and transmitted to it. This helps to explain a resistance that is usually remembered only as quaint. Some towns kept two clocks running side by side, or fitted a public dial with an extra hand so that the sun's reckoning and the railway's could be read together, and some local worthies denounced the new hour as an imposition. It is easy to read them as people clinging to habit in the face of progress. But they had grasped something that the language of convenience obscures: a shared standard is also a centre of authority, and agreeing to it means accepting that the definition of an everyday reality will henceforth be made by people one will never meet. None of this is a case against standard time, whose benefits were real and soon taken for granted. Few people today would wish to return to a world in which the hour changed as one rode across a county. The argument is rather that the history of timekeeping is also a history of who is entitled to say what time it is, and that this question did not disappear when it was settled. Each later standard, from time signals broadcast by radio to the clocks that now synchronise themselves silently over networks, has extended the same arrangement, and each has made it a little harder to notice.
R04-F-04: A familiar story about the history of reading holds that, for most of antiquity and much of the Middle Ages, people could read only aloud, and that silent reading was a late discovery which transformed the inner life of the West. The story is usually supported by a much-cited anecdote in which an ancient writer records his surprise at finding a learned man reading without voicing the words. It is a vivid story, and like many vivid stories it has been asked to carry more weight than it can bear. Scholars who have examined the evidence more closely have found a fair number of ancient readers who read silently, and they point out that surprise at a practice is not evidence that it was unknown, only that it was unusual where it was observed. The more defensible claim is not that silent reading was impossible but that it was not the default. Texts were frequently written without spaces between words, which made voicing them a useful aid, and, more importantly, reading was often a social act. A household, a monastery or a circle of friends would gather while one person read to the others; a book was something one heard as often as something one saw. What changed, then, was less the technique than the setting. As books became cheaper and more numerous, as spaces between words and other aids to the eye became standard, and as people of moderate means came to have rooms, or at least corners, to themselves, reading moved from the common table to the private chair. Freed from the pace of the voice, the eye could also move faster, and a reader alone could get through more books, and more kinds of book, than a listener ever could. The shift was gradual and uneven, and reading aloud never vanished. Families read novels to one another well into the age of print, and workers in some trades paid a colleague to read to them while they laboured. Even corrected in this way, the history matters. A text that is heard together is interpreted together: listeners react, object and argue, and the meaning of a passage is settled, if it is settled at all, in company. A text read alone is answerable only to its reader, who may skip, reread or linger over a sentence that no one else will ever know about. It would be too much to say that private reading created the private self. It would be too little to say that it changed nothing about how people came to think of their thoughts as their own.
R04-F-05: It is easy to write the history of urban smell as a simple story of progress. Pre-modern cities stank of sewage, tanneries, slaughterhouses and unwashed bodies; reformers built drains and water supplies; the stench retreated. Every part of this is true, and anyone inclined to romanticise the crowded streets of earlier centuries should be reminded of it. But the story assumes that the nose is a constant instrument, registering the same smells with the same disgust in every age, and that assumption does not survive a reading of the sources. Residents of older towns certainly complained about smells, but their complaints were selective. Odours that later generations would find unbearable, such as the smell of a dung heap beside a house, were often accepted as part of ordinary life, while others, associated with particular trades or with neighbours who were disliked, drew sustained protest. What made a smell intolerable depended less on its strength than on what it was thought to mean. And from the late eighteenth century onwards, in much of Europe, smells came to carry a very specific meaning with new urgency. Under the old theory that disease spread through foul air, now taken up by physicians and reformers, a bad smell was not merely unpleasant; it was a warning, perhaps even the danger itself. The theory was wrong, but it was productive. Because it identified smell with sickness, it gave reformers a reason, and a sense of urgency, to remove the sources of smell, and many of the measures they took, from covered sewers to the regular removal of refuse, did reduce disease, though for reasons they did not understand. A mistaken idea about how illness spread thus helped to justify works whose real benefit lay elsewhere. When the germ theory displaced it, smell lost its medical authority; it did not lose its power. Freed from medicine, the vocabulary of smell attached itself more firmly to persons. Middle-class households that had learned to fear foul air now learned to fear the odour of the poor, the newcomer and the manual worker, and the judgement passed easily from bodies to character. The cleaner cities became, the more a lingering smell could serve as a mark of social distance. This is why a history of smell cannot be only a history of drains; it must also be a history of who was allowed to call whom offensive, and of how a sense that seems the most immediate of all has always been schooled.
R04-F-06: The phrase most people use for the overland trade between China and the Mediterranean is a nineteenth-century coinage, and it carries a picture with it: a single road, and on it long caravans of camels carrying silk from one end of Asia to the other. The picture is attractive and largely misleading, for very few goods, and fewer merchants, made the whole journey. What existed instead was a chain of overlapping regional circuits, each worked by traders who knew their own stretch of desert, mountain and oasis intimately and knew little of what lay beyond it. In such a system a bale of silk might change hands many times between the place where it was woven and the place where it was worn. Each exchange added a margin, which is one reason why goods from the far end of the chain were so costly, and each was made between people who had reason to trust one another because they met repeatedly. The merchant in an oasis town did not need to know the distant market where the silk would end up; he needed to know the caravan leader who would buy it from him and the one who had sold it to him. Long-distance trade, on this view, was an accumulation of short-distance relationships. This has consequences that the romantic image hides. First, the system was more resilient than a single road would have been: when war or banditry closed one segment, goods could often find a way round it through neighbouring circuits, and trade slowed rather than stopped. Second, knowledge travelled poorly along the chain even when goods travelled well, and buyers at one end often held fanciful beliefs about where their luxuries came from, because no one they dealt with had seen the source. Third, those who profited most were frequently neither the producers nor the final buyers but the middlemen at the junctions where circuits met, whose cities grew rich on the margin. It would be wrong to conclude that no one crossed the whole distance. Pilgrims, envoys and a few adventurous traders made extraordinary journeys, and some left accounts that are still read. But these travellers are remembered precisely because they were exceptional, and their fame has shaped our picture of the ordinary trade far more than the ordinary trade itself, which left few memoirs. A history built on the exceptional journey will see a road; a history built on the routine exchange will see a web, and it is the web that explains how the trade actually worked.
R04-F-07: Two stories are commonly told about the measures that late medieval and early modern cities took against plague. In the first, the health boards of the Italian city-states, with their isolation hospitals, their passes for travellers and their periods of enforced seclusion for ships and households, are the ancestors of modern public health: rational officials confronting an epidemic with the tools of an emerging state. In the second, the same measures are a chapter in the history of coercion, in which the sick and the poor were locked away, their goods burned and their livelihoods destroyed by authorities who feared contagion more than they valued the people who might carry it. Each story can be furnished with abundant evidence. What both tend to overlook is that the measures could work only with a degree of cooperation that neither officials nor force could guarantee. Quarantine depends, at its most basic, on information. A household must be shut up before the disease spreads from it, which means that someone must report the first case, and the people best placed to report it are the members of the household themselves, together with their neighbours. Every one of them had reasons to stay silent. A shut household lost its income; its members might be removed to an isolation hospital from which many did not return; its bedding and clothing might be burned. Families that concealed a death, bribed an inspector or slipped out of the city before the doors were sealed were not simply defying authority. They were responding sensibly to the costs that reporting imposed on them, and neighbours who might have informed on them faced, in their turn, the prospect of being shut up beside them. Where the measures had any success, it seems to have been because authorities, sometimes reluctantly, took on obligations in return. Some cities fed shut-up households at public expense, paid compensation for goods that had been destroyed, or relied on clergy and charitable brotherhoods to bring food, relief and reassurance to the confined. Such provisions were expensive and often inadequate, and the surviving records do not allow us to say with any confidence how much difference they made to mortality. But they changed the calculation facing a family that suspected illness, and the complaints of officials who lacked the means to provide them suggest that concealment rose when relief failed. It might be objected that this underrates force. Cities did post guards, punish concealment severely and, on occasion, execute those who broke quarantine. Yet harshness had a cost that its advocates rarely counted: the more frightening the consequences of discovery, the stronger the incentive not to be discovered, and an epidemic that goes underground is harder, not easier, to contain. A household that expected to be sealed in with its sick, guarded and fined had every reason to wait, to hide the first symptoms and to hope, and each day of waiting was a day in which the disease could travel. Severity could secure compliance from those already known to the authorities; it could not make the unknown come forward. The lesson is not that plague regulations were humane, for many plainly were not, nor that they were futile. It is that measures which depend on people revealing something about themselves are bargains, whether or not those who impose them think of them in that way, and the point is not confined to plague. Their success is limited by what disclosure costs the person who discloses, and an authority that wishes to know must first make knowing bearable.
R04-F-08: The usual history of artificial light is a history of liberation. For most of human existence the coming of darkness set a hard limit on what people could do: work stopped, travel became dangerous, and the town shrank to the circle of the hearth. Oil lamps, then gas, then electricity pushed that limit back, until the night became little more than a dimmer continuation of the day, available for labour, commerce and pleasure. The story is not false. But it treats the night as an absence, a gap waiting to be filled, and in doing so it forgets that the pre-industrial night was a time with its own rules, its own inhabitants and its own uses. In many European towns before public lighting, the night was governed differently from the day. Gates were shut, curfew bells were rung, and anyone abroad after dark without a lantern and a good reason might be stopped and questioned by the watch. The respectable stayed indoors; the streets belonged to watchmen, to those whose trades required darkness, to lovers, thieves and the young. This was not freedom in any simple sense, for the dark was also where violence went unpunished. It was, however, a separate jurisdiction, a time in which the authority of the day ran only weakly and in which much that could not be done openly was done. The first systematic street lighting was installed less to lengthen the working day than to bring this jurisdiction under control. Its sponsors spoke of safety, and they meant it, but safety meant visibility, and visibility meant that the street at midnight could be watched and policed by the same standards as the street at noon. Accounts from several cities describe crowds breaking lamps in moments of unrest, and it is tempting to dismiss this as mere vandalism. It is more plausibly read as a recognition, however inarticulate, that the lamps were an extension of an authority that the crowd had reason to resist. The lamp, in this sense, was an instrument of the day carried into the night. Yet to replace the story of liberation with a story of discipline would be to make the opposite mistake. Lighting did extend surveillance, but it also opened the night to people who had been effectively shut out of it. Respectable women, families, the elderly and the cautious could now walk to a theatre or a shop after dark, and whole new forms of sociability, from evening promenades to late markets, grew up in the lit streets. For many people the expansion of the policed night was, quite simply, an expansion of their world. The same lamp that exposed the thief to the watch made the street usable for the seamstress walking home. What lighting did, then, was neither simply to free the night nor simply to conquer it, but to abolish it as a distinct social time. The day's rules, the day's people and the day's activities spread into hours that had once belonged to others. Those who had held the dark, the watchmen, the night trades and the young, lost not their lives but their hours, and the newcomers to the lit street rarely noticed what had been displaced. Whether we count this as a gain or a loss depends largely on whom we imagine walking the street, and it is precisely the habit of imagining only one kind of walker that has made the history of light so easy to tell and so hard to tell well.
